1Purpose

This policy sets out what [Provider name] commits to. Every gets behaviour support from who are suitable, supervised and up to date. We also commit to reduce and eliminate restrictive practices. It is for participants, their families and advocates, our practitioners and managers, and the people who check our work.

2Applies to

  • Every practitioner who does specialist behaviour support for [Provider name]: employees, contractors, agency staff and a sole practitioner.
  • Every , inside or outside [Provider name], and every manager who allocates or oversees behaviour support work.
  • Every behaviour support assessment, , interim plan, comprehensive plan and plan review we do, in any setting.
  • Only a provider registered for specialist behaviour support uses this policy. A provider that only carries out behaviour support plans uses POL-BSP-01 Behaviour Support in the NDIS Policy instead.

"The Rules" in this policy means the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018.

3Commitments

C1

We will let only a person has considered suitable do a behaviour support assessment or write any part of a plan for us. This covers employees, contractors, agency staff and work done under supervision.

Answers: ←Legislation, indicator (2)Legislation (2)How we do it: →PRO-SBS-01, step 1PRO-SBS-01 step 1→PRO-SBS-01, step 8PRO-SBS-01 step 8→PRO-SBS-01, step 26PRO-SBS-01 step 26

C2

We will confirm each practitioner's suitability from the Commission's own written outcome before we give them any participant. The outcome says suitable, not suitable or unable to decide. It shows no . We record on our the outcome date, the pathway used (self-assessment or new entry-level), any conditions, and the date of any reconsideration letter. We record their capability level from their own self-assessment against the Positive Behaviour Support Capability Framework, endorsed by their clinical supervisor. The Commission does not issue or endorse levels. We also finish their worker screening and banning order checks first.

C3

We will keep each practitioner's suitability record current. We check their dates and conditions every month and search for banning orders every 3 months. We stop their assessment and plan work the same day the Commission revokes the outcome, decides they are not suitable or tells them to stop, or they cannot show us an outcome at all. An open 12-month reconsideration for a new entry-level practitioner is a monitored risk, not a stop: they keep working unless the Commission tells them otherwise.

C15

We will support each new entry-level practitioner through the Commission's 12-month reconsideration. From their first day they have a clinical supervisor at proficient level or above, a professional development plan and a written supervisor agreement. We diary the reconsideration date and make sure the self-assessment and endorsement tool are lodged before the Commission's deadline. The Commission may impose conditions on, or refuse, a new entry-level sole trader or key personnel, so we check the outcome letter for conditions before we rely on them.

4Ground rules

G1

A person waiting for the Commission's decision on their suitability may learn the Rules, shadow a practitioner and help with administration. They do not do any part of an assessment or a plan, even when supervised. Workers, families and other providers may give information and data. They do not do any part of an assessment or a plan either.

G2

Urgency is not an exception. If no suitable practitioner is free, we do not take the referral. We help the participant and the referrer find another specialist behaviour support provider.

G3

A clinical supervisor never supervises a person who supervises them. A plan that a clinical supervisor wrote is checked by a different clinical supervisor.

G4

Clinical supervision is not performance management. Facts that show poor conduct or performance move to PRO-HRM-02 Supervision and Performance Procedure. Line supervision of workers who carry out plans is recorded on FRM-HRM-05 Supervision Session Record.

G5

Supervision records name participants by only. They hold no names, addresses or health details. The participant's own file holds the detail.

G6

Only the practitioner, the clinical supervisor, the Service Manager, the Quality Manager, the Chief Executive and our auditors read a practitioner's supervision records. The Commissioner may ask for them. We keep each record for 7 years after the practitioner stops working for us (our standard). A correction is a new version with a reason. Nobody overwrites a record.

G7

Supervision time and professional development time are paid work time. For a contractor they are written into the agreement.

G8

A practitioner may raise a concern about a clinical supervisor, a manager or the Chief Executive. Nobody is disadvantaged for doing so. Decision table 4 in PRO-SBS-01 says who receives it.

G9

In a small provider one person may hold several roles. A sole practitioner engages an external clinical supervisor and a substitute in writing. The external clinical supervisor does the Service Manager's checks on the sole practitioner's own work: their outcome, their supervision and their development. Everything else the sole practitioner does themselves. The sole practitioner holds the Quality Manager role, except that the decision whether an incident is reportable is made by the external clinical supervisor with them. The external clinical supervisor signs a confidentiality undertaking. The , named in REG-GOV-01 Delegations Register, reads the quarterly review.

G10

Sometimes one person is both the Service Manager and the clinical supervisor for a practitioner. Then the Chief Executive releases that practitioner and does their monthly check.

G11

Everyone who gives out assessment or plan work reads the suitable list first. A practitioner who is not on it is not given work.

9Words we use

606 words
practitioner
in this policy, an NDIS behaviour support practitioner who works for us. The Commissioner considers the person suitable to do behaviour support assessments, including functional behavioural assessments. The Commissioner also considers them suitable to develop plans that may contain restrictive practices (the Rules, section 5).
suitability outcome
the Commission's written decision on a person's application to be a practitioner. It says suitable, not suitable or unable to decide. It shows the date, the pathway used (self-assessment or new entry-level) and any conditions. It shows no capability level. For a new entry-level practitioner the Commission writes separately to say it will reconsider the outcome after 12 months.
capability level
the level a practitioner self-assesses against the Positive Behaviour Support Capability Framework, endorsed in writing by their clinical supervisor. The four levels are core, proficient, advanced and specialist. The Commission does not issue or endorse levels, so the level is never read from the suitability outcome.
clinical supervisor
a practitioner, inside or outside [Provider name], who is at proficient level or above on their own endorsed self-assessment and trained in clinical supervision, and who provides clinical supervision.
Clinical Lead
the most senior clinical supervisor, who owns clinical practice at [Provider name] (POL-SBS-03 defines the role). In a sole practitioner provider, the external clinical supervisor.
clinical supervision
planned supervision of a practitioner's own work by a more experienced practitioner. It looks at their assessments, plans and decisions. It is not line management.
work practice
each kind of work a practitioner does for us. It covers assessments, interim and comprehensive plans, reviews, consultation, authorisation and lodgement steps, and the handover and coaching of the people who carry out plans.
caseload
every participant a practitioner has open work for.
regulated restrictive practice
one of the five practices the Rules cover (section 6). Seclusion is sole confinement where the person cannot leave, such as a locked room. Chemical restraint is medicine given mainly to change behaviour. Mechanical restraint is a device that stops or limits movement, such as a strap or bed rails used for behaviour. Physical restraint is force used to stop or limit movement. Environmental restraint limits free access to parts of the person's environment, such as a locked cupboard or fridge.
functional behavioural assessment
the process of working out the purpose behind a person's behaviour.
interim behaviour support plan
the first plan, written for a participant with an immediate need.
comprehensive behaviour support plan
the full plan that follows a behaviour support assessment, including a functional behavioural assessment.
implementing provider
a provider that carries out a participant's behaviour support plan.
start-up session
the first clinical supervision session, held before the practitioner is given any participant.
suitable list
the list in REG-HRM-02 of practitioners released to be given participants. It shows their outcome date, pathway, endorsed capability level, conditions and any reconsideration letter date.
new entry-level pathway
the Commission's suitability pathway for a person with less than 6 months of behaviour support experience or a limited portfolio of evidence. The Commission reconsiders the outcome after 12 months, by letter. The practitioner keeps working during the reconsideration unless the Commission tells them otherwise.
file number
the number we give a participant's record. Supervision records use it in place of a name.
participant
in this policy, any person with disability we provide supports or services to.
the Commission
the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission. The Commissioner is its head.
independent contact for concerns
in a provider with one owner, the outside person who receives concerns about the owner.
business day
a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives.

1Purpose

The result: every who assesses a or writes a plan for us is confirmed suitable by . Each is supervised by a suitable and keeps their skills current. The Rules are applied in every plan, and restrictive practices are reduced and eliminated.

This procedure gives effect to POL-SBS-01 Behaviour Support in the NDIS Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support), commitments C1 to C15.

"The Rules" in this procedure means the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018.

"The Commission" is the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission.

2When and who

Start this procedure when:

  • we engage, employ or contract a practitioner or a clinical supervisor
  • a session is due
  • a practitioner's changes or is due to be reconsidered
  • a quarter ends, or the Rules change.

Who acts:

  • The Service Manager confirms suitability, names the clinical supervisor, releases the practitioner and keeps the dates.
  • The clinical supervisor holds each session, checks the plans and reviews restrictive practices.
  • The practitioner brings their work and tells us the same day of any change to their outcome.
  • The Quality Manager checks for changes to the Rules.
  • The Chief Executive reports to the governing body.

In a small provider one person may hold several roles. A sole practitioner engages an external clinical supervisor and a substitute in writing (step 4). The external clinical supervisor does the Service Manager's checks on the sole practitioner's own work: steps 1 to 3, 8, 23, 24 and 26. Everything else the sole practitioner does themselves, including the register entries (step 22), the briefing (step 28) and the Quality Manager's and the Chief Executive's steps. The one exception is the decision whether an incident is reportable, which the external clinical supervisor makes with them. The , named in REG-GOV-01 Delegations Register, reads and signs the quarterly summary (step 30).

If one person is both Service Manager and clinical supervisor for a practitioner, the Chief Executive does steps 8 and 23 for them.

3Before you start

  • Our registration includes specialist behaviour support. Check the certificate of registration. Without it, nobody assesses a participant or writes a plan (Practice Standards Rules, section 7(3)).
  • You know the practitioner's name and the date they will start.
  • You can open REG-HRM-02 Training and Competency Register, REG-HRM-01 Worker Screening Register and REG-SBS-01 Behaviour Support Plan Register.
  • You have a blank FRM-SBS-01 Behaviour Support Clinical Supervision Record. Open one at step 1 for each new practitioner.
  • For a session, you have the practitioner's list by and the drafts or plans for checking. You also have the use data for each and their development log.
  • The practitioner sends these 2 before the session (our standard).
  • You have a copy of the Rules and of the restrictive practice authorisation law of [state or territory].
  • You have the Commission's phone number, 1800 035 544, and the email address of its practitioner team, ndispractitioners@ndiscommission.gov.au.

4Watch out

  • A person who is not yet considered suitable must not do any part of an assessment or a plan, even when supervised. The Rules say a practitioner must provide the specialist behaviour support services (section 17). A plan written by anyone else breaches our registration, and it may put a restrictive practice in place that no suitable person has checked.
  • A supervisor below the level in Decision table 1 does not count as clinical supervision. The practitioner is then unsupervised in practice, whatever the diary says. Stop the session and use the substitute.
  • A plan with a regulated restrictive practice that skips the check has never been tested against the Rules. It can be lodged with the Commissioner and relied on by the people who carry it out.
  • A supervision record is not an incident report. The Commission's clock for a reportable incident runs from the day we become aware, and waiting for the next session loses days.
  • A participant's name in a supervision record spreads private information to more readers. Use the file number only.

5Steps

Confirm suitability before any work

Step 1

Service Manager

Ask the practitioner for the Commission's written suitability outcome.

Ask every new practitioner, whether employee, contractor or agency. Open FRM-SBS-01 for them. Copy from the outcome its date, the decision (suitable, with or without conditions), the pathway used (self-assessment or new entry-level) and any conditions. The outcome shows no . The level comes from the practitioner's own self-assessment against the Positive Behaviour Support Capability Framework, endorsed by their clinical supervisor, and is recorded at step 4. For a new entry-level practitioner, ask for the Commission's reconsideration letter and copy its date and deadline. Check that the name matches their identity documents. Read the result with Decision table 2.

Result
You hold the outcome, or you know there is none.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q2, Q6, Q7 and Q8
Time limit
Before the practitioner is given any participant (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support Rules, s 17 and s 18)

Step 2

Service Manager

If the outcome is missing or unclear, or a new entry-level reconsideration deadline has passed with no decision from the Commission:

Confirm the outcome from the Commission's own evidence.

The primary evidence is the outcome letter the practitioner downloads from the Commission's provider portal. Sight it and write the date you saw it. If it is missing or unclear, the practitioner asks the Commission's practitioner team by email and shows you the reply; write the date and any reference. The Commission runs no provider-facing confirmation service, so allow time. Do not accept the practitioner's word alone.

Result
You have seen the Commission's own evidence, or you know there is none.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q8

Step 3

Warning. Worker screening, banning orders and professional registration keep people who must not do this work away from participants. A practitioner who has not cleared them is unsafe to allocate, even when the Commission considers them suitable.

Service Manager

Confirm the pre-engagement checks are complete.

For an employee, use PRO-HRM-01 Human Resource Management Procedure and FRM-HRM-01 Worker Screening and Credential Checklist. For a contractor or agency practitioner, use PRO-HRM-07 Contractor and External Provider Verification Procedure, which also sets their written agreement. The checks are a current worker screening clearance for this risk assessed role. They also include a search of the NDIS Provider Register for a banning order under every name the person has used. Check qualifications, and professional registration where the profession needs it.

Result
Every check is complete and in date, or the practitioner is not given any participant.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q9
Time limit
Before the practitioner starts any work (Practice Standards (Worker Screening) Rules, s 13)

Carries out: ←Policy, commitment 2Policy C2Written on: →FRM-SBS-01, question 9FRM-SBS-01 Q9

Set up supervision and development

Step 4

Service Manager

Name the clinical supervisor and a substitute.

Use Decision table 1 for the level each must hold. Levels are read from each person's self-assessment against the Positive Behaviour Support Capability Framework, endorsed by their own clinical supervisor, never from the Commission's outcome. Record the practitioner's endorsed level, who endorsed it and the date at FRM-SBS-01 Q6. Each supervisor must be trained in clinical supervision and must not supervise anyone who supervises them. Each declares any conflict of interest on FRM-GOV-01 Conflict of Interest Declaration Form. If no one inside can do it, engage an outside clinical supervisor in writing. The agreement covers confidentiality, the NDIS Code of Conduct, how they raise a concern and who owns the records. For a new entry-level practitioner it is the supervisor agreement the Commission expects, and the supervisor is at proficient level or above. A sole practitioner engages the outside supervisor. Add an outside clinical supervisor to REG-GOV-01 Delegations Register as the holder of the position, with the substitute as first delegate.

Result
The practitioner has a named clinical supervisor and a named substitute who meet the standard.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q6 and Q10 to Q13, and REG-GOV-01 Delegations Register (position holder and first delegate) for an outside supervisor
Time limit
Before the (our standard)

Step 5

Clinical supervisor

Hold the start-up session with the practitioner.

Agree how supervision will work. Cover how often (Decision table 1), how long and how it is held. Cover how the practitioner asks for an extra session and how they raise a disagreement. Say what stays confidential and its limits: duty of care, the law and audits. Record the answers on FRM-SBS-01 as a start-up session. Keep that record open until step 8.

Result
The practitioner and the clinical supervisor have a written arrangement.

FRM-SBS-01 Q1, Q3 and Q14

Before the practitioner is given any participant (our standard)

Step 6

Clinical supervisor

Agree the practitioner's professional development plan.

Set the hours from Decision table 1 for the next 12 months. Name the topics. At least half are on positive behaviour support or other evidence-informed behaviour support practice. Use the higher number if the practitioner's professional body asks for more. Supervision sessions do not count towards the hours. Agree the dates and who pays or allows the time.

Result
There is a dated plan the practitioner can follow.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q15 and REG-HRM-02

At the start-up session, then every 12 months (our standard)

Step 7

Clinical supervisor

If the practitioner is new to us, 12 months have passed since their last Rules check, or the Rules have changed:

Check that the practitioner understands the Rules.

The practitioner first completes training on the Rules. Then they show you they can explain and apply them, using a plan of theirs or a sample plan. They must cover the five kinds of regulated restrictive practice and the conditions in section 21. They must cover the plan deadlines, consultation and notice, the approved form and lodgement, and the duty to reduce and eliminate. They must also cover the duties of , and the note for each state or territory where they work. This is the one annual knowledge check: it also serves POL-SBS-02 C2 and PRO-SBS-02 step 2, and is recorded once, on FRM-HRM-07 Training and Competency Assessment Record and in REG-HRM-02. If they do not meet it yet, agree what to learn and repeat the check.

Result
The practitioner has passed a recorded check on the Rules, or does not work alone.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q16
Time limit
Before their first assessment or plan work, then every 12 months (our standard)

Carries out: ←Policy, commitment 8Policy C8Written on: →FRM-SBS-01, question 16FRM-SBS-01 Q16

Step 8

Service Manager

Release the practitioner by adding them to the .

Release them only when steps 1 to 7 are recorded. Write the release date on FRM-SBS-01, with any limits from the conditions on the outcome. Then the clinical supervisor and the practitioner sign the start-up record, which is signed here and not at the end of the session. The practitioner then does only the work the conditions allow. Add them to the suitable list in REG-HRM-02, with their outcome date, pathway, endorsed level, conditions and any reconsideration letter date. Everyone who gives out assessment or plan work reads that list first.

Result
The practitioner is on the suitable list and can be given participants.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q17
Time limit
The day the Rules check is passed (our standard)

Run each clinical supervision session

Step 9

Clinical supervisor

Confirm that the practitioner's suitability is unchanged and that the supervision meets the standard.

Ask the practitioner to confirm the date, the pathway and the conditions on their outcome, any reconsideration letter, and whether their endorsed self-assessment has changed. Compare them with the last record. If nothing has changed, record "No change" at Q7; Q6 to Q13 then stand as last recorded. Check that you still meet Decision table 1. Ask whether you or the practitioner have a conflict of interest with any participant on today's list. If anything has changed, use Decision table 2. If you do not meet the standard, stop and use the substitute.

Result
The record shows the practitioner's suitability and the supervisor's level on the day of the session.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q1, Q3, Q4, Q6, Q7 and Q10 to Q12
Time limit
At the start of every session, no later than the longest gap in Decision table 1 after the last one (our standard)

Step 10

Clinical supervisor

Review the actions from the last session.

Go through each action and mark it done, open or overdue. For an overdue action, ask why and agree a new date. Never delete an earlier due date.

Result
Every earlier action has a status.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q5
Time limit
At the start of every session (our standard)

Step 11

Clinical supervisor

Review each participant's work that the practitioner brought.

Use file numbers only, never names. For each, write the kind of work, the plan version and what you decided. Read each handover and training record (FRM-SBS-04) and review record (FRM-SBS-05) made since the last session. Then list every participant on the caseload who has not been discussed in the last 3 months. Put each one on this agenda if there is time, or fix a date.

Result
Every participant on the caseload has been discussed within 3 months, or has a date.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q18 and Q19
Time limit
Every participant at least once every 3 months (our standard)

Carries out: ←Policy, commitment 6Policy C6Written on: →FRM-SBS-01, question 18FRM-SBS-01 Q18→FRM-SBS-01, question 19FRM-SBS-01 Q19

Step 12

Clinical supervisor

Check which plans and reviews are overdue or due soon.

Read the engagement dates and plan dates in REG-SBS-01. The Rules set these deadlines. After a regulated restrictive practice is used, the clocks start when we are engaged to write the plan. An interim plan is due within 1 month. A comprehensive plan is due within 6 months (section 19). A comprehensive plan that contains a regulated restrictive practice is reviewed at least every 12 months, and sooner after a change that needs the plan amended (section 22). For every other plan a 12-month review is our standard, and an interim plan's review date is the comprehensive plan's due date. A plan with a regulated restrictive practice is lodged with the Commissioner "as soon as practicable" (section 24(1)). The Rules use those words. Our working limit is 5 business days from the day the plan is finalised. List what is overdue or due in the next 4 weeks, with the action to meet each. Ask which plans you checked earlier have been lodged.

Result
No deadline is missed without someone knowing and acting.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q20 and Q21
Time limit
At every session (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support Rules, s 19, s 22 and s 24(1))

Carries out: ←Policy, commitment 9Policy C9Written on: →FRM-SBS-01, question 20FRM-SBS-01 Q20→FRM-SBS-01, question 21FRM-SBS-01 Q21

Step 13

Warning. A plan with a regulated restrictive practice can limit a person's freedom for years. A plan that has not been checked against the Rules can break them and still be lodged and relied on.

Clinical supervisor

Check that each plan was checked against the Rules before it was finalised.

List each plan finalised or reviewed since the last session, and each draft waiting. A plan with a regulated restrictive practice has its own recorded test. Find the clinical supervisor's decision at FRM-SBS-02 Q28 and Q29, under PRO-SBS-02 Restrictive Practices Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support). For a review, find the check on FRM-SBS-05, under PRO-SBS-04 Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure. The check must be dated before the plan was finalised. For any other plan that Decision table 1 names, test every row of Decision table 3 yourself. Approve a plan only when every row passes. Otherwise return it with the changes needed, or hold it. If a plan with a restrictive practice was finalised with no recorded check, tell the Service Manager the same day. Do the test now and raise an entry in REG-QMS-01. A plan you wrote is tested by a different clinical supervisor. If the practitioner disagrees with your decision, see "If it goes wrong".

Result
Each plan has a recorded check dated before it was finalised, or a gap that is being fixed.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q22 and Q23
Time limit
At every session. A draft with no recorded check is tested within 5 business days of arriving, or 2 business days for an interim plan (our standard)

Step 14

Clinical supervisor

Review the regulated restrictive practices on the practitioner's caseload.

For each practice, read the use data since the last session and the trend. Ask what reduction step was agreed, who takes it and by when. Ask whether any use was an emergency use, or was outside the plan or outside an authorisation, and what followed. Send any such use to the Service Manager the same day (Decision table 4). Do not accept "no change" as a default. Ask what must happen first and fix a date to look again.

Result
Each practice has a reduction step with an owner and a date, or a reason and a date to look again.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q24 to Q26
Time limit
At every session (our standard)

Step 15

Clinical supervisor

Observe or read a sample of the practitioner's own work.

Choose one. Sit in on a consultation or an assessment visit. Watch a recorded session, with consent. Or read a full draft assessment, plan or data analysis. Pick work you have not seen before. Write what you saw and what you found. This shows that supervision looks at the work, and not only at the practitioner's account of it.

Result
The clinical supervisor has seen the practitioner's work first hand.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q27
Time limit
At least once every 3 months (our standard)

Carries out: ←Policy, commitment 6Policy C6Written on: →FRM-SBS-01, question 27FRM-SBS-01 Q27

Step 16

Clinical supervisor

Give the practitioner feedback on their work.

Name what they do well and what to build, with an example for each. Include comments from participants or their representatives. Seek those comments at least once every 12 months. Then ask what the practitioner thinks of their caseload and of this supervision, and write down their reply.

Result
Your feedback and the practitioner's views are on the record.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q28 and Q29
Time limit
At every session (our standard)

Written on: →FRM-SBS-01, question 28FRM-SBS-01 Q28→FRM-SBS-01, question 29FRM-SBS-01 Q29

Step 17

Clinical supervisor

Ask the practitioner about their wellbeing and any need for a debrief.

This work is hard. Always ask after a serious incident, a use of a restrictive practice or a distressing consultation. Offer a debrief and a referral to [employee assistance or other support]. Do not wait for the next session when the need is urgent.

Result
Wellbeing has been asked about and any support is agreed.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q30
Time limit
At every session, and a debrief within 2 business days when asked for (our standard)

Written on: →FRM-SBS-01, question 30FRM-SBS-01 Q30

Step 18

Clinical supervisor

Record the professional development the practitioner has done.

Write each activity with its date, hours and topic since the last session. Add the total for this 12 months and compare it with Decision table 1. If the practitioner is behind, agree dated catch-up steps. Note any training they need, so the Service Manager can update their training plan in REG-HRM-02.

Result
The hours and progress are known, and training needs reach the training plan.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q31 and REG-HRM-02
Time limit
At every session (our standard)

Carries out: ←Policy, commitment 11Policy C11Written on: →FRM-SBS-01, question 31FRM-SBS-01 Q31

Step 19

Warning. A supervision record is not an incident report. Waiting for the next session to report a safety or reportable matter can make a notice to the Commission late.

Clinical supervisor

If the session raised a safety, conduct, reportable or Rules compliance concern:

Start the process that Decision table 4 names.

Phone the person the table names. Then write on FRM-SBS-01 what you did and give the number of the incident report, complaint or other record. The Quality Manager decides whether an incident is reportable and notifies the Commission. The Commission's clock runs from the day we become aware: within 24 hours of becoming aware where the incident involves the death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact or sexual misconduct of a participant, or an unauthorised restrictive practice that resulted in harm; otherwise within 5 business days (Incident Management and Reportable Incidents Rules, s 20 and s 21). A worker must tell a supervisor or manager "as soon as possible" (section 19). Our standard is the same day.

Result
The concern is in the right process, and the record shows which.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q32 and Q33
Time limit
The same day (our standard)

Carries out: ←Policy, commitment 14Policy C14Written on: →FRM-SBS-01, question 32FRM-SBS-01 Q32→FRM-SBS-01, question 33FRM-SBS-01 Q33

Step 20

Clinical supervisor

Agree the new actions and the next session date.

Give each action one owner and a due date. Set the next date no later than the longest gap in Decision table 1. Put it in both diaries before the practitioner leaves.

Result
Everyone knows what happens next and when.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q34 and Q35
Time limit
At the end of every session (our standard)

Carries out: ←Policy, commitment 5Policy C5←Policy, commitment 7Policy C7Written on: →FRM-SBS-01, question 34FRM-SBS-01 Q34→FRM-SBS-01, question 35FRM-SBS-01 Q35

Step 21

Clinical supervisor and practitioner

Sign the record.

Each person signs, or confirms electronically with their name, date and time. Do not change a signed record. Add a correction as a new version, with the reason.

Result
The record is complete.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Sign-off
Time limit
The same day, and no later than 1 business day after the session (our standard)

Carries out: ←Policy, commitment 7Policy C7

Step 22

Service Manager

Enter the session in REG-HRM-02.

Enter the date, the supervisor and their endorsed level, the development hours and the next due date. Note whether the session was on time. Enter no participant names. File the signed record in the practitioner's supervision file.

Result
The register shows the session and the next due date.
Record
REG-HRM-02
Time limit
2 business days after the record is signed (our standard)

Carries out: ←Policy, commitment 7Policy C7

Keep suitability and development current

Step 23

Service Manager

Check each practitioner's dates in REG-HRM-02.

Read the suitable list and look for six things. First, a new entry-level reconsideration deadline within 3 months: ask what the practitioner has lodged with the Commission (the self-assessment and the endorsement tool), and look again every month. Second, an outcome the Commission has revoked, limited or questioned, or an endorsed self-assessment missing: use Decision table 2. Third, a session overdue past the longest gap in Decision table 1: see "If it goes wrong". Fourth, a Rules check due within 1 month: book step 7. Fifth, development hours behind the plan at 6 months or 12 months: ask the clinical supervisor to agree catch-up steps. Sixth, a supervisor or substitute who no longer meets Decision table 1.

Result
Nothing is about to lapse unseen.
Record
REG-HRM-02
Time limit
Every month (our standard)

Carries out: ←Policy, commitment 3Policy C3←Policy, commitment 5Policy C5←Policy, commitment 8Policy C8←Policy, commitment 11Policy C11and 1 more

Step 24

Service Manager

Search the NDIS Provider Register for banning orders against each practitioner and clinical supervisor.

Search every name each person has used. The Register must list a person who has a banning order in force (NDIS Act 2013, section 73ZDA(3)). Save a dated copy of each result. If you find a banning order, use Decision table 2 at once and tell the Chief Executive.

Result
There is dated evidence that no banning order was in force on the day of the search.
Record
REG-HRM-02
Time limit
Every 3 months (our standard)

Carries out: ←Policy, commitment 3Policy C3

Step 25

Behaviour support practitioner

If the practitioner learns that the Commission has changed, ended or questioned their outcome, or that their worker screening clearance or professional registration has changed:

Tell the Service Manager.

Say what changed, on what date and what the Commission or registration body said. Send a copy of any letter. Do no assessment or plan work that the change may not allow until the Service Manager answers.

Result
The Service Manager knows on the day.
Record
None
Time limit
The same day (our standard)

Carries out: ←Policy, commitment 3Policy C3

Step 26

Service Manager

If the Commission has revoked, limited or ended the outcome, decided the practitioner is not suitable or told them to stop, or the practitioner cannot show an outcome at all, or a banning order, screening or registration problem bars the work:

Stop the practitioner's assessment and plan work.

Tell the practitioner and the clinical supervisor. Move each participant's work to a released practitioner, so no deadline in the Rules is missed. Tell each participant, or the person who represents them, who their practitioner is now. Tell the Chief Executive. For a banning order, stop all their work with participants. Take the practitioner off the suitable list. Hold a session of the kind "Review of the arrangement" within 3 business days. The practitioner goes back on the list only after steps 1 to 8 are repeated.

Result
Nobody does assessment or plan work without a suitability outcome the Commission has not revoked, and every participant has a practitioner.
Record
FRM-SBS-01 Q1 and Q17
Time limit
The same day (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support Rules, s 17 and s 18)

Apply the Rules and reduce restrictive practices

Step 27

Quality Manager

Check for changes to the Rules and the authorisation law.

  • A session is missed. Rebook it within 5 business days (our standard). If two sessions in a row are missed, the Service Manager tells the Chief Executive. No plan with a regulated restrictive practice is finalised until a session is held.
  • A deadline in the Rules will be missed. The practitioner tells the Service Manager at once. The Service Manager moves the work to another released practitioner within 2 business days (our standard), tells the participant and records the cause in REG-QMS-01. A missed section 19 deadline is a breach of a condition of our registration (NDIS Act 2013, section 73J), not a notifiable event in the Rules. If a deadline has already passed, the Chief Executive decides whether to self-report to the Commission's behaviour support team by email, and records the decision, the reason and the REG-QMS-01 entry that shows the correction.
  • The practitioner disagrees with the clinical supervisor's decision on a plan. The plan is not finalised while the disagreement stands. The Service Manager asks a second clinical supervisor at the same level or above to read it within 5 business days (our standard).
  • The outcome cannot be confirmed in time. The practitioner is not released. Tell the referrer and the participant the same day, and help them find another specialist behaviour support provider.
  • A concern is about a colleague, a manager or the Chief Executive. Use Decision table 4. Nobody is disadvantaged for raising it.
  • The Service Manager is the clinical supervisor, or the provider has one owner. See "When and who".

docs.html:
1Purpose

The result: a goes into a 's behaviour support plan only after the participant and the people they choose have been consulted. They know the risks and the alternatives. The practice meets the Behaviour Support Rules and the authorisation process of the state or territory. The plan also holds a way to reduce the practice and end it.

This procedure gives effect to POL-SBS-02 Restrictive Practices Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support), C1 to C15.

"The Behaviour Support Rules" here means the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018. A "practice" is a regulated restrictive practice, one of the five kinds in section 6 of those Rules. A "restrictive practice" in the wider sense is any practice or intervention that has the effect of restricting the rights or freedom of movement of a person with disability (NDIS Act 2013, section 9); a practice is regulated only if it meets section 6. A "plan" is an interim or a . A "high-risk practice" is one the NDIS Commission's guidance says must never be in a plan (POL-SBS-02 C15).

2When and who

Start this procedure when any of these happens:

  • A Behaviour Support proposes a practice for a new interim or comprehensive plan.
  • A plan review adds, changes or removes a practice.
  • Someone tells you a practice is in use for a participant we write plans for.
  • 3 months have passed since our notes, our practitioners' learning and our open practice records were last checked (step 30).

Who acts:

  • The Behaviour Support Practitioner leads at steps 1, 2, 4 to 7, 9 to 21, 23 to 27 and 29, and lodges the plan (step 24).
  • The Clinical Supervisor decides whether the practice goes into the plan (step 22). The Clinical Supervisor also keeps the notes and the learning current (steps 3 and 30).
  • The Service Manager opens the response to unauthorised use (step 8), prepares the lodgement and keeps its date and reference (step 24), and copies the record to the REG-SBS-01 Behaviour Support Plan Register practice sheet (step 28).
  • The Chief Executive hears about missed due dates and concerns about managers.
  • The Quality Manager decides whether anything we find is a reportable incident for us, and notifies the NDIS Commission.

Only a provider registered for specialist behaviour support uses this procedure. A provider that only carries out plans uses PRO-BSP-02 Regulated Restrictive Practices Procedure.

In a small provider one person may hold several roles. REG-GOV-01 Delegations Register shows who holds each role. A sole practitioner is also the Service Manager, the Quality Manager and the Chief Executive, except that the decision whether an incident is reportable is made by the outside Clinical Supervisor with them. The Clinical Supervisor is never the practitioner who proposed the practice. A sole practitioner engages an outside Clinical Supervisor in writing before taking any plan that may hold a practice; the outside Clinical Supervisor also does the Service Manager's checks on the sole practitioner's own work.

3Before you start

  • You are a Behaviour Support Practitioner: the Commissioner has considered you suitable to do assessments and write plans that may hold a practice.
  • The plan has a row in REG-SBS-01. The row shows the date we were engaged. It shows when the interim plan is due (1 month after) and when the comprehensive plan is due (6 months after).
  • You have the referral, the assessment so far, and the incident and use records from each .
  • You can open the participant's communication preferences. They are in FRM-RGT-01 Communication, Advocacy and Support Preferences Form.
  • You can open the participant's consent record. It is in FRM-INF-01 Consent to Collect, Use and Share Information Form.
  • You can open REG-QMS-03 Compliance Obligations Register and REG-HRM-02 Training and Competency Register.
  • You have a blank FRM-SBS-02 Restrictive Practice Consultation Record.

4Watch out

  • A signature is not an authorisation. The participant's, a guardian's and ours do not make a practice lawful. Only the authorisation process of the state or territory does. A practice used without it breaches the registration conditions and can be a reportable incident.
  • Never include a practice the state or territory prohibits. The implementing provider is bound not to use it (Behaviour Support Rules, section 8). A plan that directs it puts the participant at risk and the provider in breach.
  • Never include a high-risk practice the NDIS Commission says must never be in a plan: prone or supine restraint, a pin-down or take-down, a restraint that restricts breathing or circulation, a punitive or aversive practice, over-correction or the seclusion of a child. State or territory authorisation never makes one acceptable. Decision table 2 row 16 tests this first.
  • Silence is not agreement, and being told is not understanding. A person who nods may not have understood. A plan built on that is built on a view the participant does not hold.
  • The plan clocks run while you consult. The interim plan is due 1 month after we are engaged. The comprehensive plan is due 6 months after (Behaviour Support Rules, section 19). Shortening the consultation to meet a date harms the participant and breaks the Rules.
  • Only a prescriber decides what a medicine is for, and what dose. You never decide or change a dose. The plan's chemical restraint protocol copies the medication, dose, route and frequency exactly from the prescriber's current order and names the prescriber and the date of the order; this consultation record holds no dose. A wrong decision about a medicine can seriously harm the participant.
  • A single emergency use needs no authorisation first, but it is still a reportable incident. If more use is likely, the participant needs an interim plan (Behaviour Support Rules, sections 9 and 19; Incident Rules, section 16). Handle it at step 7.
  • A practice is never a punishment, a convenience or an answer to short staffing. Any of these is a reason to refuse the proposal.
  • Telling someone the participant has refused can break their trust and their privacy. Contact only the people they chose, plus the person with legal authority and the providers who may use the practice, whom the law requires us to consult. Record each refusal and its reasons: that record is our evidence of all reasonable steps under section 20(3)(e).
  • If anyone is in immediate danger, call 000 first. Then follow PRO-INC-01 Incident Management Procedure.

5Steps

Get ready

Step 1

The Behaviour Support Practitioner

Open a consultation record for this participant and plan.

Use FRM-SBS-02. Start a new record for each new plan, and for each review that adds, changes or removes a practice. Write the plan number from REG-SBS-01. Read the due dates in that row and plan your meetings to fit them.

Result
One consultation record exists for the plan and links to its row in REG-SBS-01.
Record
FRM-SBS-02 Q1
Time limit
Before you talk with anyone about the practice (our standard)
Step 2

The Behaviour Support Practitioner

Check that your learning and the state or territory note are both current.

Read your row in REG-HRM-02. You need the annual knowledge check under PRO-SBS-01 step 7, which covers the Behaviour Support Rules, the section 21 conditions, the note for this state or territory and the duties of implementing providers, and you need learning on restrictive practices and their risks. Each date must be within the last 12 months. Also copy your pathway (self-assessment or new entry-level) and your endorsed from FRM-SBS-01 Q6, so the Clinical Supervisor can set the scrutiny at step 22. Then open the note in REG-QMS-03. Its last-checked date must be within the last 6 months, and the note must have been re-checked after any announced change to the law, the authorising body's process or its guidance. Copy the dates to the record. If the practice will be used in two states or territories, check both notes.

Result
You know whether you may propose a practice, and which authorisation process applies.
Record
FRM-SBS-02 Q2 and FRM-SBS-02 Q3
Time limit
Before you propose a practice (our standard)
Step 3

The Clinical Supervisor

If your learning or the note is out of date, or there is no note for the state or territory:

Bring the learning or the note up to date.

For learning, book the knowledge check under PRO-SBS-01 step 7 or a learning session, and record the date and result in REG-HRM-02; the knowledge check is recorded once, on FRM-HRM-07 Training and Competency Assessment Record, and serves both procedures. For a note, use Decision table 4. Write it from the authorising body's current published guidance and the law of the state or territory. Ask the authorising body when anything is unclear. The practitioner does not propose or finalise a practice until this is done.

Result
The practitioner may go on, with learning and a note that are both current.
Record
FRM-SBS-02 Q2 and FRM-SBS-02 Q3. The note is kept in REG-QMS-03 and the learning in REG-HRM-02
Time limit
10 from the day the gap is found (our standard)

Name the practice and find its status

Step 4

The Behaviour Support Practitioner

Decide which kind of practice it is, using Decision table 1.

Describe what is done, where, when, by whom and for how long. Take this from the referral and the use records, not from the name people give it. The primary purpose decides the kind. If the practice fits none of the five kinds, tell the Clinical Supervisor. The Clinical Supervisor decides whether it is a regulated restrictive practice under section 6 and, if not, whether the state or territory regulates it, and records why. When you are unsure, treat it as regulated. Check the practice against the high-risk list in POL-SBS-02 C15: a high-risk practice is never proposed, whatever a state or territory authorises.

Result
The practice is described in plain words and its kind is recorded.
Record
FRM-SBS-02 Q4
Time limit
Before you meet anyone to consult (our standard)
Step 5

Warning. Only a prescriber decides what a medicine is for and what dose to give. A wrong decision about a medicine can seriously harm the participant.

The Behaviour Support Practitioner

If the practice involves a medicine or a device:

Sight the current prescription or medication chart, and ask the prescriber or the treating health practitioner to confirm in writing what the medicine or device is for.

Ask whether its primary purpose is to influence behaviour, or to treat a diagnosed condition or enable treatment. Record the medicine or device, the prescriber or health practitioner, and whether it is given routinely or only as needed. Record the date of the written answer. Do not write a dose, a time or a rate in this record. They stay in the prescriber's order, and the plan's protocol copies them from there exactly. Until the written answer arrives, treat the medicine or device as a regulated practice for planning purposes. Send the step 7 letter only once the prescriber confirms the primary purpose is behavioural, or has not answered within 2 business days of being asked.

Result
The record shows whether the medicine or device is a regulated practice, and on whose word.
Record
FRM-SBS-02 Q5
Time limit
Ask within 2 business days of step 4 (our standard)
Step 6

The Behaviour Support Practitioner

Check whether the practice is in use now, and whether the state or territory prohibits it.

Ask each implementing provider whether it uses the practice, and read its use records. Compare what you find with the note. Is the practice authorised now, in which plan, on what conditions and until when? Then read the note's list of prohibited practices and 's high-risk list. A single emergency use needed no prior authorisation but is still a reportable incident for the provider that used it: record it and go to step 7 so the provider's report can be checked. Write what you find with its source and date.

Result
You know the status of the practice before you consult anyone.
Record
FRM-SBS-02 Q6 and FRM-SBS-02 Q7
Time limit
Before you meet anyone to consult (our standard)
Step 7

Warning. Every use of a practice that is not authorised, or not in the plan, may be a reportable incident. A delay in telling the implementing provider leaves the participant exposed and delays its notice to the NDIS Commission.

The Behaviour Support Practitioner

If the practice is in use without authorisation, or outside the plan, or the state or territory prohibits it, or it is a high-risk practice. For a medicine or device, only once the prescriber has confirmed the purpose is behavioural or has not answered within 2 business days:

Tell each implementing provider in writing what you found.

Say which practice, where and when you saw it, and why it is not authorised or not in the plan. For a prohibited practice, say that it must not be used. Ask whether the provider has made its report to the NDIS Commission. Send a copy to the Service Manager. Write the date and time you sent it.

Result
The implementing provider knows, in writing, and the Service Manager has been told.
Record
FRM-SBS-02 Q6 and FRM-SBS-02 Q7
Time limit
The same business day you find it (our standard)
Step 8

The Service Manager

If the practice is in use, and it is unauthorised, outside the plan or prohibited:

Open the response under PRO-SBS-05 Reportable Incidents Involving the Use of a Restrictive Practice Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support).

Write the PRO-SBS-05 record number at Q6. The implementing provider reports its own use to the NDIS Commission; the Quality Manager decides whether the matter is also a reportable incident for us. The practitioner carries on with this procedure for the plan. Where the participant is at risk now, the practitioner also starts the interim plan route. That is PRO-SBS-06 Interim Behaviour Support Plans Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support).

Result
The response to the unauthorised use has started and can be traced to this record.
Record
FRM-SBS-02 Q6
Time limit
The same business day you are told (our standard)

Involve the people

Step 9

The Behaviour Support Practitioner

Ask the participant who they want involved, and what they need to take part.

Read their communication preferences first. Arrange what they need: their format, an interpreter, a cultural support person, a support person, a quiet place, a time of day. Ask about each person and provider by name. Record each yes and each no in FRM-INF-01. Offer an independent advocate and write down the answer. Do not contact anyone the participant refused, except the person with legal authority and the providers who may use the practice (steps 10 and 16). Record each refusal with the participant's reasons: that is our evidence of all reasonable steps under section 20(3)(e), and the Clinical Supervisor records at step 22 whether any further step is reasonable.

Result
The participant has chosen who takes part and has the supports they need.
Record
FRM-SBS-02 Q8 and FRM-SBS-02 Q9
Time limit
Before you give notice or consult anyone (our standard)
Step 10

The Behaviour Support Practitioner

Confirm who has legal authority over a decision about the practice.

Presume the participant decides. Ask whether a guardian, an administrator, a person with parental responsibility for a child, a tribunal or an authorised officer holds authority. Sight the document. Write what it covers, its date and any expiry. For a parent, record the basis of parental responsibility and any court order that changes it. For a child in statutory care, the delegate of the Minister or agency decides: sight the delegation. Tell the participant that you must consult this person even if they said no, and why. If you cannot see a document, or it has expired, do not treat the person as holding authority. Ask the authorising body what it needs. If the participant cannot decide and nobody has authority, stop and tell the Service Manager (PRO-BSP-03 Decision table 2).

Result
The record names who decides, on what authority, and the participant knows it.
Record
FRM-SBS-02 Q10
Time limit
Before you give notice at step 11 (our standard)
Step 11

The Behaviour Support Practitioner

Give written notice of the intention to include the practice.

Ask them to tell you, show you or point to what could go wrong. Write what they said or did. If they have not understood, explain again a different way, with a different support. Each person has heard the alternatives, and the record shows which came first.

FRM-SBS-02 Q15

In the same meeting as step 12 (our standard)

The Behaviour Support Practitioner

Strategies exist that were built with the people involved, and they come first.

Each implementing provider knows what data to keep and what help it will get.

The Clinical Supervisor holds everything needed to decide.

Decide

A second qualified person has tested the practice, and the decision and its reasons are written.

Everyone consulted knows the outcome and the reasons for it.

FRM-SBS-02 Q30

Within 5 business days of the decision (our standard)

Step 24

The Behaviour Support Practitioner. The Service Manager prepares the lodgement

Lodge the plan with the Commissioner.

The Commission's portal requires the Practitioner to send the lodgement; the Service Manager may enter the data and prepare the draft, and the Practitioner checks it and sends it. The Commissioner holds the plan.

Within 5 business days of the plan being finalised (our standard). The Behaviour Support Rules, section 24(1), say as soon as practicable (statutory)

The Behaviour Support Practitioner

If the note says the state or territory has an authorisation process for this practice:

Seek authorisation by the route the note sets.

Follow the note. Where we apply, send the plan and the evidence the note lists. Where the implementing provider, a guardian or the participant applies, give them the plan and the evidence and write down who applies. Include the participant's view and any objection in full. The authorising body, or the person who applies, has what is needed.

FRM-SBS-02 Q32

Within 5 business days of the Clinical Supervisor's decision to include (our standard)

The record shows whether the practice may be used, on what conditions and until when.
Record
FRM-SBS-02 Q33

The same business day you learn the outcome (our standard)

Each implementing provider holds its duties and the limits of the authorisation in writing.

Within 2 business days of each entry (our standard)

Every gap has an owner and a date, and the notes and learning are current.

form.intro:
Use this record for every clinical supervision session of a behaviour support practitioner. It shows who supervised, whether the practitioner is suitable and current, what work was checked and what was decided.

The completes it during the session, with the practitioner. Both sign on the day. Complete one record for each of these:

  • a start-up session, held before the practitioner is given any participant
  • every planned session
  • every extra session the practitioner asks for
  • every review of the arrangement after a change in the outcome, the level or the supervisor.

Only a specialist behaviour support provider uses this record. Line supervision of workers who carry out plans is recorded on FRM-HRM-05 Supervision Session Record.

Have these ready: the practitioner's caseload list by file number, the plans for checking and the use data for each regulated restrictive practice. Also have their development log, the Commission's suitability outcome, any reconsideration letter and their endorsed self-assessment against the Positive Behaviour Support Capability Framework. The Service Manager completes Section B from these before a start-up session. At a planned session Section B is not re-entered: the clinical supervisor confirms "No change" at Q7, or records what changed.

Three answers are gates. A "No" at Q11 stops the session until the substitute takes it. A return or hold at Q22 means the plan is not finalised. A "Yes" at Q32 starts a step in PRO-SBS-01 Behaviour Support in the NDIS Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support) the same day.
form.privacy:
This record holds information about a practitioner's work, suitability and development. It names participants by file number only. We collect it to show that each practitioner is suitable, supervised and learning, and that the plans we write meet the Rules.

The practitioner, the clinical supervisor, the (the most senior clinical supervisor, who owns the Module 2A clinical documents), the Service Manager, the Quality Manager, the Chief Executive and our auditors read it. The NDIS Commissioner may ask for it: giving the Commissioner information on request is a condition of our registration (NDIS Act 2013, section 73F(2)). We store it in the practitioner's supervision file, not in a participant's file. We keep it 7 years after the practitioner stops working for us (our standard). The practitioner can ask to see their record and ask us to correct it. POL-INF-01 Information Management Policy sets how we store it.
form.after:
1. The clinical supervisor and the practitioner sign the record on the day of the session. The latest is 1 business day after (our standard). A start-up record stays open and is signed when the practitioner is released.
  2. The clinical supervisor files the signed record in the practitioner's supervision file the same day it is signed.
  3. The Service Manager enters the session in REG-HRM-02 Training and Competency Register within 2 business days of the signing (our standard).
  4. If Q32 is "Yes", the clinical supervisor has already started the process in Decision table 4 of PRO-SBS-01. The Service Manager reads the record within 1 business day and confirms what was done.
  5. If Q22 shows a return or a hold, the clinical supervisor tells the practitioner the same day. The plan is not finalised until it is checked again.
  6. The Quality Manager reads a sample of records every 3 months. Any record with "No" at Q11 or "Yes" at Q32 is always in the sample.
  7. A sole practitioner's external clinical supervisor does the Service Manager's part of this routing. The Quality Manager's sample is read by a second practitioner from outside the business: the external clinical supervisor's named substitute, or another practitioner the sole practitioner engages for the purpose. The reads only the quarterly summary and any concern raised.
form.signoff:
Both people sign the same day. A confirmation from each person in the system, with their name, date and time, counts as a signature. A start-up record is signed when the practitioner is released (PRO-SBS-01 step 8).
